name: Vacheeswarar Temple, Tirupachur
deity: Shiva as Vacheeswarar (Pachuranathar), with the goddess Thangaathali (Pasupati Nayaki)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Tondai country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with Chola-era and later additions
dynasty: Chola patrons (tradition names Karikala Chola) and later
summary: Vacheeswarar is an ancient Shiva temple of the Tondai country praised in the Tevaram, where the Lord is worshipped as a self-risen linga found in a grove of bamboo, and the goddess Thangaathali is honoured as the one the Lord took to himself as his own beloved.

sections.history: Tirupachur stands in the Tondai country of northern Tamil Nadu, a short way west of Tiruvallur on the road that runs towards Tiruttani. It is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the Shiva shrines sung by the Tevaram saints, and tradition remembers the hymns of Tirunavukkarasar, the saint Appar, and of Tirugnana Sambandar here, which carries the temple's fame back to the seventh century. By old account the place was once a dense forest of bamboo — pachu in the speech of the country — where the Lord revealed himself as a swayambhu linga, a form not made by human hand, and from this he is called Pachuranathar, the lord of the bamboo grove. Local tradition credits the early Chola kings, and Karikala Chola above all, with raising the temple in stone after the linga was found in the forest, and the complex keeps inscriptions of the Chola age that speak to its long standing.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east in the Dravidian manner, its gateway tower opening onto a walled enclosure with the pillared halls and corridors of a long-settled shrine. In the sanctum the Lord is worshipped as a self-risen linga, said to bear a mark from the time it was uncovered from the earth, for which reason the deity is traditionally honoured without being touched in the daily rites. The goddess Thangaathali, also named Pasupati Nayaki, is enshrined in her own hall, and the temple is known for a gathering of eleven forms of Ganesha set together within the precinct. A Srichakra held by tradition to have been installed by Adi Shankara is kept here, and an image of the goddess as Swarna Kali is venerated within the walls. Much of the present fabric is modest in scale but old in feeling, a village sanctuary grown around a sacred spot rather than a towering monument.
sections.legends: Several stories gather at Tirupachur. In one, Vishnu is said to have worshipped Shiva at this place to regain his purity after his long battle with the demons Madhu and Kaitabha. The story the temple holds dearest is the goddess's own: she is said to have undertaken severe penance to win the Lord, and when he appeared and received her he called her en kadhaliye, my own beloved, so that she is honoured here as Thangaathali, the beloved one, and her shrine is sought by those who pray for loving union and married life. Tradition further holds that Adi Shankara, passing through, established a Srichakra at the shrine, and that the fierce goddess Swarna Kali was calmed and settled here under the watch of Nandi. These accounts are carried in the temple's local tradition and in the Sthala Purana.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, is the temple's foremost festival, kept through the night with worship and the offering of lamps. The monthly Pradosham, at dusk on the thirteenth lunar day, draws devotees as at every Shiva shrine, and the usual Tamil observances of the Shaiva year are followed. Because the calendar of festivals follows the Tamil months and local custom, dates and the fuller round of annual celebrations are best confirmed with the temple before a visit.
sections.experience: Tirupachur rewards an unhurried visit as a quiet country shrine rather than a crowded pilgrimage centre. Enter through the eastern gateway, come before the self-risen linga of Vacheeswarar in the sanctum, and then turn to the goddess Thangaathali in her own shrine, whom devotees approach with prayers for love and the harmony of the home. Many pause before the gathered forms of Ganesha within the precinct. The village lies off the busy road between Tiruvallur and Tiruttani, and within its walls the temple keeps the stillness of a very old sacred place set among the fields of the Tondai country.

visit.timings: Generally open in the morning and again in the late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; reported hours differ between sources, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirupachur lies about 5 km west of Tiruvallur on the road towards Tiruttani, near the Kadambattur junction, and roughly 60 km from Chennai. Kadambattur, on the Chennai suburban railway line, is the nearest station, and Chennai has the region's international airport. Buses along the Tiruvallur–Tiruttani road serve the village.
